paper_title: SynthDCB: World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Scaling device-control evaluation requires scaling both interactive worlds and the tasks agents must solve. We introduce SynthDCB, a benchmark for environment awareness and device control built through world distillation (WD). World distillation transforms knowledge of device behaviors, constraints, and environmental effects into modular executable components. A unified capability representation connects tool discovery, world execution, and task synthesis. SynthDCB instantiates Home, Car, and Phone with 114 device classes, 1,166 functions, and 95 events, supporting five task families with 32 subtypes. Explicit states and tool-call traces support task validation and agent evaluation. We evaluate 22 models on 2,560 test tasks; the best achieves 88.8% mean Pass@1. Construction experiments demonstrate token efficiency and expansion of task coverage. At the richest knowledge level, WD fully covers 22/23 properties, 19/29 functionalities, and 30/39 event requirements specified in a real RobotVacuum protocol. Furthermore, the 1,000 sampled tasks semantically cover 81.6% of the 854 reference instructions in the real-world corpus. SynthDCB connects an expanding space of real-to-sim executable capabilities to verifiable agent evaluation.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Tool-using agents are advancing rapidly and integrated into voice assistants in home, car, or mobile phones, accompanied by growing collection of benchmarks and executable environments for evaluating their capabilities (Yao et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2025; Seo et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b). At the same time, device manufacturers and system developers continually introduce new devices and expand their functionality. When simulation environments do not keep pace, the capabilities covered during agent training and evaluation can lag behind those required in deployment. This creates need for benchmarks that can be rapidly extended as new device capabilities emerge, both to evaluate agents against evolving requirements and to support iterative agent training. Meeting this need requires addressing two connected challenges. On the construction side, adding device capability requires consistent tool interfaces, behavior implementations, world configurations, 1 : World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking Figure 1: Overview of SYNTHDCB. SYNTHDCB builds configurable executable worlds from reusable device capabilities across Home, Car, and Phone. Agents interact with these worlds through device tools and are evaluated on tasks involving environment states, user preferences, and temporal dynamics. The example shows coordinating an air conditioner with washer cycle to reach Alexs preferred temperature at the required time. task requirements, and success criteria; generating more instructions over an unchanged environment does not expand what the benchmark can execute. On the evaluation side, agents must understand and operate the environment presented to them, rather than merely invoke controls in fixed configuration. This requires discovering available devices and operations, interpreting the current world state, and determining which parts of user request can be satisfied. An extensible benchmark should therefore support both the introduction of new executable capabilities and the assessment of environment understanding and device control across different worlds. Consider the request: Cool the bedroom to 22 before 22:00, and turn on the bedside lamp at 20% brightness. Changing an air conditioners setpoint is not the same as bringing the room to the requested temperature: the latter depends on environmental dynamics, and meeting the deadline also depends on when actions are taken. If the cooling requirement is infeasible in the current world, the lighting requirement may still be achievable. Evaluating these distinctions requires explicit action effects, temporal evolution, and success conditions for individual requirements. We therefore ask: How can we rapidly extend executable device environments and verifiable tasks to evaluate agents ability to understand and control unfamiliar worlds? We introduce the world distillation (WD) pipeline that transforms behavioral knowledge into reusable executable components for constructing worlds and their tasks. Typed capability specifications guide component implementation and validation, define discoverable tool interfaces, and provide the operations used by task builders. World composition assembles these components into domainspecific layouts or module structures. Execution-grounded task synthesis derives requirements from available capabilities and checks candidate tasks through reference-execution replay. Once validated, component can be reused across world configurations and task instances without reimplementing its behavior again. This supports on-demand device expansion, while configurable worlds enable evaluation of how agents explore and use the capabilities of the devices instantiated for each task. We instantiate this approach as SYNTHDCB, covering Home, Car, and Phone with 114 device classes, 1,166 functions, and 95 events. The benchmark supports five task families with 32 subtypes, combining state queries, device control, environmental goals, and coordinated execution. Evaluation of 22 models on 2,560 test tasks yields best mean Pass@1 of 88.8%. Model rankings vary across domains. Larger models perform well on direct device control but struggle primarily with interpreting complex user 2 : World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking intent and coordinating subtasks to fulfill the complete request. Smaller models face more basic challenges in following interaction protocols and selecting appropriate tools to complete individual atomic tasks. Construction experiments with Codex using the same GPT-5.6 Sol demonstrate the scalability and efficiency of world distillation. Building all three domains consumes 19.16M tokens at an estimated cost of $120.09 before cache discounts within couple of hours, automating specification, implementation, testing, and repair that could otherwise require over month of manual work. In the RobotVacuum comparison, WD achieves broader complete capability coverage than Codex low at comparable token budgets under richer knowledge inputs, and uses 51.5-86.7% fewer tokens per completely covered requirement than Codex xhigh across three knowledge levels. With full-protocol input, 1,000 generated RobotVacuum tasks cover 81.6% of 854 reference instructions and 69.8% of 172 categorized intents. These results connect efficient capability construction to broader task coverage, demonstrating the scalability of world distillation. We summarize our contributions as follows: An extensible environment and world distillation pipeline. We design stateful simulator with explicit device behaviors, shared environmental effects, and temporal dynamics, together with pipeline that transforms device knowledge into executable components and validated tasks. benchmark and evaluation of 22 models. We introduce SYNTHDCB across Home, Car, and Phone, with five task families covering 32 subtypes. Evaluation on 2,560 test tasks and detailed failure analysis expose distinct gaps in environment awareness and reliable device control. An analysis of construction scalability and efficiency. We quantify domain construction costs, stage execution, and capability coverage under different knowledge inputs. Comparisons with Codex demonstrate efficient expansion of executable behaviors, providing foundation for broader evaluation and capability transfer.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Tool-use benchmarking. Tool-use research evaluates and trains agents to complete tasks through external APIs. Call-oriented benchmarks assess tool selection and argument construction (Li et al., 2023; Patil et al., 2025), while synthesis methods generate tool-use supervision (Qin et al., 2024; Prabhakar et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025). Stateful benchmarks evaluate execution consequences through policy-constrained interactions (Yao et al., 2024; Barres et al., 2026), state dependencies and trajectory milestones (Lu et al., 2025), or state checks (Trivedi et al., 2024). Device control further requires modeling how multiple operations affect shared environment states over time. Device-control agents and environments. Device-control benchmarks examine instruction understanding, environment discovery, and coordinated execution. Existing approaches emphasize command validity, grounded control, and personalized assistance (Li et al., 2025; Rivkin et al., 2023; Bharadwaj et al., 2026). SimuHome and SMH-Bench introduce home simulators for temporal workflows and contextual reasoning (Seo et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b), while VehicleWorld and DevicesWorld extend evaluation to in-car interaction and heterogeneous device workflows (Yang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026a). As device capabilities evolve, these environments must expand their executable behaviors together with the tasks that exercise them. Table 1 situates SYNTHDCB among related benchmarks. SYNTHDCB combines coverage across 3 domains with extensible device behaviors and verifiable tasks, allowing new capabilities to enter evaluation through shared world distillation pipeline. Scalable executable environments and tasks. Environment and task synthesis expands agent training and evaluation while aligning tasks with executable outcomes. Environment-centered 3 : World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking approaches generate environments alongside tasks or verifiers (Hu et al., 2025; Song et al., 2026; Dong et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026); other methods organize function dependencies or combine procedural homes with executable goals (Maekawa et al., 2026; Gu et al., 2026). Scaling device worlds additionally requires reusable behaviors that interact through shared state and simulated time. SYNTHDCB addresses this through world distillation: device knowledge becomes executable components, world composition instantiates their interactions, and task synthesis derives verifiable requirements. Each new component can thus expand both the environment and its task inventory.

This design lets new device model support many worlds and user requests.

sections.title: 3.3 Task Construction
sections.content: Capability-grounded sampling. Each instantiated world supplies shared capability inventory of queryable properties, device operations, processes, and candidate environmental goals. Builders efficiently reuse this inventory and cached execution previews to produce batches of tasks from the same world or valid initial-state variants. Table 2 summarizes the five task families. Target devices or spaces can be selected directly, through environment exploration, or through filtering and comparison queries from object pool; target values can come from legal samples, relative changes, queried values from value pool, or memory. Queries that determine later targets or values become explicit prerequisite atom tasks. Goal builders probe executable space change plans, while Aggregate builders combine validated components from the same initial state after checking read/write conflicts and target compatibility.

sections.title: 4.1 Dataset and Splits
sections.content: SYNTHDCB covers Home, Car, and Phone with 114 device classes and 1,166 tools. Its current evaluation splits contain 314 validation tasks (150 Home, 105 Car, and 59 Phone) and 2,560 test tasks (1,281 Home, 768 Car, and 511 Phone). Both splits are sampled disjointly from shared pool of 30,309 tasks constructed from 130 worlds. We use the validation set to compare 8 instruction styles across 9 models, and evaluate 22 models on the test set with conversational style to reflect most frequent everyday requests. The test set includes 2,289 feasible, 170 infeasible, and 101 partial tasks, with memory requirements in 200 tasks. Appendix reports detailed statistics of SYNTHDCB.

sections.title: 4.2 Agent and Interaction Protocol
sections.content: All evaluated models1 use the same ReAct-style agent (Yao et al., 2023) and interact with SYNTHDCB through iterative observations and actions. Agents use system-level tools to discover environmental rules, available devices, and function schemas, then use this information to select target devices and construct function calls in subsequent turns. Query answers use session.submit_answer, one per question in instruction order with required JSON types. Each infeasible or blocked atom task needs session.submit_report with status, reason code, and explanation; partial tasks also require completing all independently executable atom tasks. 1Temperature is 0 and top-p is 1. Response limits are 1,024 tokens for local-deployed models, and 16,384 for API served models, while all other parameters remain at their default values. 7 : World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking Simulated time advances through configured action/turn costs (inactivated by default) and session.sleep_time. Agent interaction ends when the agent calls session.finish or reaches the 20-turn limit. For tasks containing Goal or Workflow atoms, background simulation continues without further agent actions to the tasks fixed evaluation horizon. Other tasks are evaluated immediately when interaction ends. We provide further analysis of interaction budgets in 4.6.

sections.title: 4.3 Evaluation Metrics
sections.content: We use mean Pass@1(%) as main metric, where successful attempt must pass all applicable state, answer, report, memory, and temporal/workflow checks. For partial/infeasible tasks we also report reason-code accuracy (RC) and semantic report pass rate (Sem.). For memory-related tasks we report separate success rates for memory-conditioned (Read) Control/Goal and memory-write (Write) atoms. Eff-A and Eff-T count satisfied state assertions and exactly matched query answers per tool call and interaction turn, respectively, for further tool call efficiency inspection. Full metrics are defined in Appendix B.6.

sections.title: 4.4 Main Results
sections.content: We present the main results in Table 4. Recent closed-source models demonstrate strong performance: Gemini 3.8 Flash leads overall at 88.8%, followed by GPT-5.6 Terra (82.6%), GPT-6 Astra (82.0%), and GPT-6.1 Sol (81.7%). Rankings vary across domains, with Gemini leading Home and Car at 86.5% and 87.0%, while Astra leads Phone at 98.2%. Small open-weight models struggle with task completion: the evaluated MiniCPM5 and Gemma-4 variants achieve only 1.6-8.7% mean Pass@1, revealing substantial gap in reliable control on edge devices. 8 : World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking Similar performance conceals distinct strengths and failure modes. Contemporary GPT models across capability tiers achieve similar overall success rates, with Astra performing better on feasibility assessment, coordination of partially executable requests, and memory use. GPT-5.6 Terra, however, has substantial advantages on counting (Q5) and enumeration (Q6), achieving 90.6% and 85.5%, compared with Astras 37.5% and 4.3% (Figure 9). The case study in Appendix D.3, Case 9, connects Astras low enumeration score to its interpretation of the output requirements: 129 of its 132 failed attempts contain the correct target list together with an extra baseline answer. The agent treats an intermediate lookup as an additional query to answer. This pattern suggests that stronger reasoning does not necessarily translate into higher task success when output requirements are misinterpreted. Figure 3: Cost-performance tradeoff across API models. Efficiency and cost at similar performance. Beyond these task-specific differences, we examine interaction efficiency, measured by Eff-A and Eff-T, alongside inference cost in Figure 3. GPT-6.1 Terra achieves similar overall success rate to GPT-5.6 Sol (79.5% vs. 79.1%), with higher Eff-A and Eff-T at only about 31% of Sols cache-discounted inference cost. Appendix details the cost calculation. These results show that similar overall success rates can be achieved with greater interaction efficiency and substantially lower inference cost. 4.5 Instruction-Style Ablation We evaluate 9 models across 8 instruction styles on validation set (Figure 4). Direct instructions (S2) achieve the highest average Pass@1, improving GPT-5.6 Luna by 7.0 percentage points over Template (S1). This pattern favors clear, explicit wording that reduces semantic ambiguity and the need to infer task requirements. Average performance declines with colloquial Folk instructions (S6) and falls sharply under Implicit instructions (S8). S6 preserves concrete requirements despite informal phrasing, whereas S8 deliberately leaves more details unstated. Distracting instructions (S7) remain broadly comparable to Conversational instructions (S5), suggesting relative robustness to irrelevant asides for most of the models. Table 13 provides the complete results. Implicit instructions still permit partial achievement of task requirements. From S1 to S8, Astras Pass@1 drops by 36.3 pp (-44.7%), whereas device-property accuracy, answer accuracy, and list-answer recall decline by 22.8 pp (-23.2%), 14.4 pp (-15.4%), and 13.1 pp (-13.3%), respectively  (Table 14)  . These smaller declines indicate that the model still achieves parts of the user intents even when it cannot satisfy the original targets whose details have been omitted. sections.title: 4.7 Error Analysis
sections.content: We analyze failed first attempts across all 22 models using 12 categories in four groups  (Table 20)  , with each attempt contributing total weight one across its ordered causes. Consistent with the main results, stronger models execute individual device operations reliably but struggle with interpreting complex requests and coordinating subtasks. Task understanding and coordination (E6) account for 73.5% and 75.2% of weighted failures for GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra, respectively. Dynamic and temporal reasoning (E10) also accounts for 9.3% of weighted failures within Workflow tasks, highlighting the demands of timing and synchronization. Smaller models face more basic barriers in following interaction protocols (E2) and constructing valid tool calls (E3), which can prevent even individual subtasks from being completed. E2 alone accounts for 96.8% of Qwen3.5-2Bs weighted failures. Appendix provides the attribution protocol and representative case studies. 10 : World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking

sections.title: 5 World Distillation Scalability and Efficiency Analysis
sections.content: Capability coverage and token efficiency. To quantify the efficiency of world distillation, we compare World Distillation (WD) and Codex on constructing RobotVacuum class from scratch with three levels of external knowledge: brief description (L1, 0.06k chars), functional overview (L2, 0.77k chars), and complete protocol knowledge (L3, 89.8k chars). We also summarized capability requirements from the full protocol. Both methods use GPT-5.6 Sol, with Codex evaluated at low and xhigh reasoning effort. Experiment settings are detailed in Appendix A.5. As shown in Table 5, WD uses 0.9-66.0% and 46.2-92.5% fewer tokens than Codex low and xhigh across the three knowledge levels. At comparable token budgets, WD achieves higher complete coverage than Codex low across properties, functions, and effect/event requirements at both L2 and L3. Compared with Codex xhigh, WD uses 51.5-86.7% fewer tokens per completely covered requirement. At L1, the brief description provides little protocol detail, and all methods achieve limited coverage. WDs coverage advantage emerges with richer knowledge at L2 and L3.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion and Future Work
sections.content: We introduced SYNTHDCB, scalable benchmark for environment awareness and device control across Home, Car, and Phone. World distillation converts device knowledge into reusable executable components for world and task construction ( 3.2, 3.3). The benchmark combines diverse tasks, shared interaction protocol, and state and process checks ( 4.1, 4.2, 4.3). Evaluation of 22 models yields best mean Pass@1 of 88.8%, while similar overall scores conceal differences in capabilities, efficiency, and cost ( 4.4). Instruction-style analysis favors explicit wording and reveals partial task achievement under implicit requests ( 4.5). Failure analysis distinguishes protocol and tool-use barriers in smaller models from complex intent interpretation and coordination failures in stronger models ( 4.7). The budget analysis shows that agents often continue interacting after their actions suffice for eventual Goal attainment, with limited gains beyond 20 turns for most selected models ( 4.6). Construction experiments demonstrate efficient capability expansion and broader instruction and intent coverage with detailed protocol knowledge ( 5). Future work will explore targeted training with generated tasks to improve the reliability and efficiency of smaller models for on-device deployment. 13 : World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking

sections.title: Ethics Statement
sections.content: Human Involvement All human-involved checks, including inspection of generated artifacts, were conducted by the authors. No crowdworkers or students participated in this work. Privacy SYNTHDCB uses synthetic simulated device worlds. Scenario object identifiers, initial states, target states, and user instructions are artificial and are not linked to real people, households, or devices. The auxiliary RobotVacuum coverage analysis uses reference instructions from the external knowledge. These materials are distinct from the synthetic benchmark tasks and from personal user interaction logs. Generated artifacts undergo schema validation, replay validation, and author inspection; any personally identifying content encountered is excluded. Intended Use and Potential Risks SYNTHDCB provides benchmark code, generated device-class specifications, simulated scenarios, tool schemas, reference trajectories, supervised tool-call records, and evaluation scripts for benchmark evaluation and controlled agent-training research. Generation is constrained to daily device-control operations over predefined device properties and functions, and invalid or offensive generated content is excluded if encountered during validation and inspection. Results on SYNTHDCB measure tool-use competence in simulated environments and do not establish readiness for real-world autonomous device control. Direct transfer to physical systems, especially appliances, vehicles, locks, heating systems, and other safety-critical devices, may introduce safety risks. Real-world deployment requires independent safety validation, permission management, human oversight, rollback mechanisms, and domain-specific constraints on high-risk actions. Licensing Publicly released artifacts will be accompanied by license or terms-of-use file. External models and software artifacts are used under their respective licenses or provider terms, and proprietary models are accessed through API services. sections.title: A World Distillation
sections.content: A.1 Capability Specification and Interfaces device specification contains metadata, properties, functions, and events, with optional inheritance and process declarations. Properties declare their type, default, access mode, units, and admissible values. The implementation supports booleans, integers, numbers, strings, and structured collections. Numeric declarations can specify bounds, step origins, and precision; collection declarations specify their structure. Read-only, read/write, and disabled properties are distinguished explicitly. Inheritance resolves updates and disabled members before the effective specification is used for code generation or loading. Functions declare JSON parameter schema, mutation status, read and write sets, and semantics such as observation, assignment, collection mutation, or process control. Preconditions and argument sources connect those operations to the state they require. The loader checks that referenced properties exist and that the declaration agrees with the implementation. For an instance exposing subset of properties, function is exposed only if all its declared property dependencies are present. This rule also determines which actions task construction can use. Events describe continuous effects, effects following an action, or responses to declared dependencies. Home space effects operate on temperature, humidity, illuminance, noise, and air quality; each domain catalog determines its own legal targets and units. Phone modules update local state and declared dependencies without Home space effects. Optional process specifications describe modes, phases, phase durations, and persisted progress variables. Public methods return status and response; event hooks return status and list of effects. A.2 Component Generation and Repair Generation is organized around artifacts with explicit dependencies. The type inventory and placement constraints identify candidate components. The metadata stage combines the request, domain property catalog, inherited specification, schema, and retrieved references. Template assembly constructs the class and property wrappers, after which code completion implements public actions and event hooks. Test generation uses the specification and implementation to exercise valid calls, invalid inputs, boundary conditions, power behavior, and effects. The production gate performs deterministic schema and declaration checks, inspects generated source against its execution restrictions, checks specificationimplementation consistency, and executes generated unit tests in an isolated subprocess. Errors are returned to the earliest relevant stage, preserving the requested capabilities and bounded repair settings. Attempt records retain failures, auxiliary generation calls, usage, and repair lineage. A.3 Runtime and Temporal Semantics The runtime executes commands against validated world and maintains separate audit of command results, state changes, and time ticks. Device actions update their own state and may emit space effects. During minute tick, hooks observe common pre-tick snapshot, and the reducer combines their effects before committing environmental updates. Contributions replace the previous contribution from the same source; additive deltas are accumulated; approach effects move baseline toward declared targets at bounded rates. The domain contract validates allowed combinations and units, then clamps and rounds values using the propertys specification. These rules define the simulators behavior abstraction and are not calibrated physical model. Command execution and time advancement use state checkpoints so rejected or failing operations do not leave partial committed updates. The simulator advances in integer minutes. Waiting, declared 19 : World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking action durations, and configured turn costs determine elapsed time; model latency does not advance the simulation clock. Independent calls can share turn, while calls requiring new observation must occur in subsequent turn. Device-tool discovery is also required in preceding turn under the benchmark configuration. The agents finish signal ends interaction immediately. When private target defines an evaluation horizon, background simulation continues to that fixed horizon without further agent actions. Goal construction derives horizon from the reference duration d: (cid:24) 2d 60 teval = t0 + max 60, 60 (cid:25)(cid:19) (cid:18) (4) . Workflow targets supply their own horizon and transition relations. The evaluation horizon remains fixed when the agent waits or finishes. The public information supplied to the agent is retained in each turns context. Without horizon, final-state checks use the interaction-end state. Previously submitted answers retain their submission-time interpretation. Workflow scoring records the first qualifying transition for each required event. Ordered relations use minute and audit sequence to disambiguate events in the same minute; other relations check bounded delays, synchronization, specified times, or strict before deadlines. The legacy target-level by/within constraint uses an inclusive deadline. This distinction is represented in the target and instruction. A.4 World and Task Construction Algorithms The world constructor samples supported layout, assigns compatible components, samples legal property values, applies initialization operations, and loads the resulting world through the shared contract. task may derive perturbed initial state from source world; its effective state is saved with the task. The following algorithm summarizes the active task-building path. 1. Load world and build an inventory of exposed properties, operations, processes, and environmental effects. 2. Sample task family and candidate requirements from that inventory. Preview operations to bind their resulting states, answers, and relevant time transitions. 3. Construct the private target and reference plan. For negative requirement, retain its construction reason; for partial task, retain executable requirements as well. 4. Replay the plan from fresh copy of the effective initial world. Run schema, public/private, instruction-alignment, termination, and evaluator checks. 5. Accept the complete bundle when its reference satisfies the target. Preserve unsuccessful candidates in the generation records. 6. Produce instruction styles from the accepted requirements, retaining the same base-task identity and paired assets. Goal probing has finite search budget. Exhausting that budget records construction failure; an unreachable-goal label requires separate construction evidence. Aggregate construction merges compatible requirements, targets, memories, and reference operations from the same effective world, then validates the merged task. A.5 Construction Experiment Setup We compare WD and Codex on RobotVacuum construction using external knowledge of varying levels of richness: short summary (L1), detailed functional description (L2), and the complete device protocol (L3). Both use GPT-5.6 Sol with identical device descriptions and framework references; 20 : World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking Codex uses low or xhigh reasoning, while WD uses the provider default. Source inspection and behavioral checks assess complete and partial coverage against common checklist summarized from the protocol. The generated RobotVacuum device is not included in the final Home domain of SYNTHDCB and is used solely for analysis purposes. Codex setting. The experiments use Codex version 0.165.1. For each experiment, we create copy containing the complete SYNTHDCB source code, expert references and domain metadata for the Home domain, and brief task instruction. We place the corresponding external knowledge in DEVICE.md in the root directory. We launch the task in /goal mode and enable Approve for me as the permission protocol. The experiments are conducted on the same local server and under the same network conditions. Cost estimation. For the Codex baselines, we measure the elapsed time from the start of goal execution to completion, along with the token usage reported by Codex. For WD, we measure the elapsed time from launching the job planner to completing the entire pipeline and count all token usage during this period, including all recorded generation, retry, review, repair, and failure-analysis calls. Token costs are calculated using details provided in Appendix E, without cache discounts. A.6 Generated-Task Coverage The external knowledge references include an instruction corpus with 861 records and 854 distinct instruction texts. We retain all 854 texts, including spatial references, gestures, following requests, clarification, and slot-filling interactions. frozen protocol-assisted taxonomy groups them into 172 intents, merging synonymous expressions and concrete parameter values while retaining actions, directions, query targets, modes, ordering, recurrence, and compound or conversational requests. Each method supplies 1,000 validated tasks at each knowledge level. At sample sizes 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, and 1,000, five samples without replacement yield the mean coverage and minimum-maximum bands ploted in Figure 7. We use GPT-6.1 Sol to match the original task templates and execution evidence against the reference instructions, preserving action and direction while abstracting concrete parameter values. Instruction coverage counts the union of matched texts. Intent coverage counts intents with at least one matched text. A.7 Additional Construction Results The source-capability checklist contains 23 property/query dimensions, 29 protocol functions, and 39 effect/event requirements. At L2, WD fully covers 18/23 property dimensions and 14/72 parameters, compared with 0/23 and 5/72 for Codex low. At L3, the corresponding results are 22/23 and 50/72 for WD, and 9/23 and 27/72 for Codex low. WD covers 23/29 action effects at both levels, compared with 14/29 and 12/29 for Codex low. It also fully covers five of eight temporal effects and both required events. The execution probes show timed cleaning, pause/resume, scheduled starts, and progressive charging in WD-L2. WD-L3 supports ten process modes with their required arguments. Remaining gaps include incompatible optional-argument combinations and missing schedule triggers. The original Codex-L2 constructor prevents World restoration; the task-coverage experiment uses its repaired copy. Codex-L3 updates battery use during cleaning but lacks the explicit sweep-then-mop transitions shown in Figure 8. : World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking

GENERAL_SYSTEM_PROMPT You are working within Device Control Bench (DCB), Pythonbased framework for simulating the functions and dynamics of everyday smart devices, such as TVs in homes, power systems in cars, and alarm apps on phones. DCB builds device domains, models, worlds, and tasks to generate benchmark data and evaluate AI agents ability to query device and space states and reliably control devices through tool calls. MODEL_GENERAL_SYSTEM_PROMPT # Device Control Bench model generation Create deterministic device models for simulated physical world used to test toolcalling agents. An Object Class is an instantiable device type. Properties hold state, public functions are the agentfacing tool API, and private ` _on_* ` events update the device's own state and may emit physical effects on the surrounding Space. ## Authority and scope Apply information in this order: 1. The current device request, representative acceptance contract, and any inherited base specification. 2. The supplied JSON schema, property runtime contract, Domain Space catalog, and generatedcode security contract. 3. Fixed and retrieved references, which are patterns only and may never override 1 or 2. An explicitly supplied acceptance contract is minimum coverage requirement. Preserve its required parent, properties, functions, disabled inherited members, events, and behavioral requirements. You may add small justified capability, but never simplify below that floor. Do not copy an example's capabilities, magic constants, or behavior unless the current device request independently requires them. Model requested Phone/Car system settings, networking, notifications, schedules, collections, and infotainment as local deterministic state. Do not invent unrelated capabilities or access real services. Phone modules have no Space and no separate electrical power switch unless explicitly requested. Car devices use only their allowed physical or functional Space; the Space owns overall results, while the Device owns control settings. Never copy Homeonly effect properties into another Domain. supplied Domain property catalog is authoritative. HOME_ENVIRONMENT_EFFECT_RULES ## Domain Space effects These rules apply to the supplied Domain catalog. Phone has no Space and emits no Space effects; its minute ticks may update its own state. Car uses the properties allowed for its actual containing Space, including functional Spaces. For Home only, the mutable Space targets are `temperature`, `humidity`, `illuminance`, `noise`, and `air_quality`. Events may implement device's own timed process even without any Space effect. Otherwise add events only for direct physical effects on those Space targets. 41 : World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking For ordinary device effects use `tick` for continuous or minutebyminute output, and `after_action` for an effect recalculated after successful public mutation that changes device state. Crossmodule dependency receivers may additionally declare dependency_changed and implement _on_dependency_changed(context). The runtime supplies context["dependencies"] keyed by source object ID, each with its declared properties. Recompute only the receiver's own state, idempotently, using internal_set; return no Space effects. The World owns contains/depends_on relations. Do not store foreign object IDs as device properties. Represent each physical effect with exactly one event trigger. sections.title: Instruction Rewriting
sections.content: The shared system template receives one of the seven style definitions below. Template instructions are generated deterministically. The user message contains the task fields and applicable context fields shown here. TASK_REWRITE_SYSTEM_PROMPT Rewrite one templatecreated DCB instruction into the requested language style. All supplied template instructions express the same task. Device references may differ because multiple names uniquely identify the same device in this world. In every style, you may choose any of these supplied references; preserve the chosen template's task information and identifying qualifiers. Do not combine the equivalent templates into additional requests. Write device and space references as natural lowercase prose without quotation marks. In direct, preserve object model property names, operation names, class/type identifiers, and literal values verbatim, including their spelling and underscores. In concise and polite, minor terminology changes are allowed, but keep all target qualifiers and task information explicit. Conversational, distracting, and folk may translate technical wording into everyday expressions with limited meaning shifts, but must retain all concrete numeric values, amounts, ranges, topk counts, and requested activities. They may shorten target references using the layout when the target remains clear. Only implicit may omit numbers, ranges, technical distinctions, and target qualifiers, expressing the broad intent through approximate or ambiguous requests. Use the supplied layout to ground these requests in the actual environment. Broader device names and contextual references are allowed. Do not invent user location or unrelated objectives. For distracting, use conversational wording and add user chatter that does not change the requested task: things the user did today, their mood, plans for tomorrow, opinions or evaluations, or meaningless expressions. The chatter may concern the current environment, other environments, the task's devices, or other devices; it does not have to be about different topic from the task. You may invent these asides, including environmental 56 : World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking observations and device anecdotes, placing them before, between, or after task clauses. They must not introduce additional requests, change task targets, conditions, or timing, invent the user's current location, or supply query answers or private memory values. Ground task targets in the supplied layout; mentioning another environment or device in an aside does not make it task target. Removing the chatter must leave the same conversational task. Other styles do not add this distracting content. An intentionally missing device/space, unsupported property/capability, or invalid literal is fixed by the template. Preserve the exact identity and offending property/value in every style, including implicit. Never invent different missing attribute during rewriting, repair the request into feasible one, or replace an actual literal such as 12 degrees with the label "invalid value". State the request without revealing its feasibility or expected report. Preserve data dependencies in every style: if Query supplies later request's target or value, that request must still use the Query result. Keep independent requests independent. Never replace failed Query with guessed target/value, drop an independent executable request, or reveal internal atom IDs, failure statuses, or reason codes in the instruction. Device Control instructions refer to the named device setting; environmental Goal instructions refer to the actual space property. For terminal Goal, use bring, reach, or match, not keep or maintain. Preserve this distinction outside the implicit style. Query answer formatting is defined by the benchmark prompt. Omit answerformat directives, including JSON serialization, answer wrapping, and sorting by names or IDs. Ranking tie handling is also defined by the benchmark prompt; omit phrases such as "including boundary ties" from the rewritten task. In every style except implicit, retain the candidate scope, ranking intent, exact topk count, and action order. Only implicit may express these more loosely while keeping the overall query or action intent recognizable. When target value comes from memory, do not state or infer its private literal value. Direct, concise, and polite must retain the savedpreference cue. Conversational, distracting, and folk may phrase it naturally, such as " Kate's usual setting", while preserving the preference source. Implicit may leave the memory cue unstated. For savedpreference Goal, ask to match that preference without spelling out evaluator tolerance amounts, tolerance ranges, or endpointinclusion rules. Every style except implicit must retain explicit goal values and ranges. Only implicit may replace them with qualitative goals such as brighter, little quieter, or comfortable. Preserve any request to create or update memory from Query result, without supplying that result in advance. Never expose internal device or space IDs. Within the instruction field, express requests in natural language, never as tool calls or API syntax. Do not encode actions using functioncall notation, empty parentheses, parameter assignments, or JSON objects. Follow the requested style's terminology and valuepreservation rules while expressing arguments in prose: for example, " set power (value=true)" becomes "set power to true", "delete clip (clip_id="clip_1")" becomes "delete clip with clip_id clip_1", and "resume guidance ()" becomes "resume guidance". Use natural singular and plural forms such as "1 minute" and "2 minutes", never the optional suffix in "minute(s)". Parentheses may clarify ordinary prose. Preserve parentheses, equals signs, or other punctuation when they belong to required literal name or text value; do not treat them as API formatting. These wording rules apply to the instruction text, not the required JSON response wrapper. Target instruction style: {instruction_style} Description: {instruction_style_description} Examples: {instruction_style_examples} Examples illustrate wording only; never copy their entities, values, or objectives into this task. An example's layout applies only to that example. Use the actual task layout when shortening references. Direct, concise, and polite retain complete task information. Conversational, distracting, and folk retain concrete values while changing expression, allowing limited everyday reinterpretation. Exact number words such as "two" for 2 are allowed outside direct; "a bit" is not substitute for concrete amount. Only implicit may transform precise instructions into vague intentbased requests without restating numbers or technical details. Keep the overall requested activities recognizable and never supply query answer in advance. 57 : World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking Respond with reasoning in <think> and exactly one JSON object in <answer> following the structure below: ```json { "instruction": <the rewritten instruction> } ``` TASK_REWRITE_USER_PROMPT The complete set of equivalent template instructions is provided below, including available devicename variants. Refer to all candidates and produce one rewrite in the requested style. Choose supplied device reference that uniquely identifies the intended target. Task id: {task_id} Task family: {task_family} Task subtype: {task_subtype} Public space and device layout (IDs identify layout entries; do not copy internal IDs into the instruction): ```json {world_layout} ``` Template instruction candidate(s): {instruction_template} TASK_REWRITE_CONTEXT Current user (use their space only for an unqualified unique device): {current_user} Unambiguous device references for this user: {public_entity_aliases} Fixed infeasible request details (preserve the request, do not expose this diagnosis): {failed_request_specs} Private dependency graph (preserve dependencies and independent requests; never expose IDs): { dependency_atoms} Requested instruction style: {style} Protected nonentity literals (preserve each verbatim): {protected_literal_anchors} Required values and constraints (numbers may use exact word equivalents): {protected_literal_anchors} Previous rewrite failed validation: {error}. Correct this issue while preserving the requested style. Use wording different from every supplied template. Failed-request and dependency fields appear for the corresponding tasks. Direct and infeasible requests use the protected-literal field; other explicit styles use the required-values field. Validation feedback is included for retries. F.2.1 Direct Style REWRITE_STYLE_DIRECT instruction_style: direct instruction_style_description: Tone: Neutral, explicit commands without conversational framing. Information: Keep every action, target qualifier, value, unit, condition, selection rule, and execution order explicit. Terminology: Preserve objectmodel property names, operation names, class/type identifiers, and literal values verbatim; change only the surrounding prose. References: Retain all supplied space, device, and person qualifiers even when the layout would allow shorter reference. Structure: State the requested actions directly in clear, complete clauses. Avoid: Greetings, courtesy phrases, informal substitutes for model terms, omitted information, and invented context. instruction_style_examples: Example 1: 58 : World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking Input: Tell me the current temperature of the space named Kitchen. Rewrite: Report the current temperature of the kitchen. Example 2: Input: For Dining Room Lamp 8, decrease brightness by 10 and increase color_temperature by 300. Rewrite: Decrease brightness by 10 and increase color_temperature by 300 on dining room lamp 8. Example 3: Input: Bring the illuminance in Stairs into line with Kate's saved preference. Rewrite: Bring the stairs' illuminance into line with Kate's saved preference. Example 4: Input: Compare current noise among Entryway, Laundry Room, Living Room; list every target in the top 2 positions for highest noise. Rewrite: Compare the current noise in the entryway, laundry room, and living room. List every space in the top 2 positions for highest noise. Example 5: Input: Please change all bluetooth speaker devices as follows: adjust playback_content upward by 2 and adjust volume downward by 10. Then tell me the current temperature in Kitchen. Then, for all living_room spaces, work toward this outcome: increase their illuminance by about 100, ending between 780 and 820. Rewrite: Increase playback_content by 2 and decrease volume by 10 on all bluetooth speaker devices. Then report the current temperature of the kitchen. Then, for all living_room spaces, increase their illuminance by about 100, ending between 780 and 820. F.2.2 Concise Style REWRITE_STYLE_CONCISE instruction_style: concise instruction_style_description: Tone: Brief, neutral instructions with minimal wording. Information: Keep every action, target qualifier, value, unit, condition, selection rule, and execution order explicit. Terminology: Allow minor, meaningpreserving wording changes, such as color_temperature to color temperature; retain the exact operation and values. References: Retain all supplied space, device, and person qualifiers; shorten wording without omitting task information. Structure: Use compact clauses, fragments, or semicolons while keeping all steps understandable. Avoid: Courtesy phrases, filler, ambiguous abbreviations, omitted qualifiers, and invented context. instruction_style_examples: Example 1: Input: Tell me the current temperature of the space named Kitchen. Rewrite: Current temperature in the kitchen? Example 2: Input: For Dining Room Lamp 8, decrease brightness by 10 and increase color_temperature by 300. Rewrite: Lamp 8 in the dining room: decrease brightness by 10; increase color temperature by 300. Example 3: Input: Bring the illuminance in Stairs into line with Kate's saved preference. Rewrite: Bring the stairs' illuminance into line with Kate's preference. Example 4: Input: Compare current noise among Entryway, Laundry Room, Living Room; list every target in the top 2 positions for highest noise. Rewrite: Among the entryway, laundry room, and living room, list the top 2 noisiest rooms. Example 5: Input: Please change all bluetooth speaker devices as follows: adjust playback_content upward by 2 and adjust volume downward by 10. Then tell me the current temperature in Kitchen. Then, for all living_room spaces, 59 : World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking work toward this outcome: increase their illuminance by about 100, ending between 780 and 820. Rewrite: All bluetooth speakers: increase playback content by 2; decrease volume by 10. Then report current kitchen temperature. Then, for all living rooms, increase illuminance by about 100, ending between 780 and 820. F.2.3 Polite Style REWRITE_STYLE_POLITE instruction_style: polite instruction_style_description: Tone: Courteous, natural dialogue, more formal than conversational or folk. Information: Keep every action, target qualifier, value, unit, condition, selection rule, and execution order explicit. Terminology: Allow minor, meaningpreserving wording changes to technical terms and operations; retain the exact operation and values. References: Retain all supplied space, device, and person qualifiers, even when the layout makes them redundant. Structure: Use clear requests such as Please, Could you, or Would you mind, with complete task details. Avoid: Excessive formality, apologies, gratitude, optionality such as if possible, omitted information, and invented context. instruction_style_examples: Example 1: Input: Tell me the current temperature of the space named Kitchen. Rewrite: Could you tell me the current temperature of the kitchen? Example 2: Input: For Dining Room Lamp 8, decrease brightness by 10 and increase color_temperature by 300. Rewrite: would like to decrease brightness by 10 and increase color temperature by 300 on dining room lamp 8. Example 3: Input: Bring the illuminance in Stairs into line with Kate's saved preference. Rewrite: Please bring the stairs' illuminance into line with Kate's preference. Example 4: Input: Compare current noise among Entryway, Laundry Room, Living Room; list every target in the top 2 positions for highest noise. Rewrite: Would you mind comparing the current noise levels in the entryway, laundry room, and living room, then listing the top 2 noisiest rooms? Example 5: Input: Please change all bluetooth speaker devices as follows: adjust playback_content upward by 2 and adjust volume downward by 10. Then tell me the current temperature in Kitchen. Then, for all living_room spaces, work toward this outcome: increase their illuminance by about 100, ending between 780 and 820. Rewrite: Please increase playback content by 2 and decrease volume by 10 on all bluetooth speakers. Then tell me the current temperature of the kitchen. After that, for all living rooms, please increase their illuminance by about 100, ending between 780 and 820. F.2.4 Conversational Style REWRITE_STYLE_CONVERSATIONAL instruction_style: conversational instruction_style_description: Tone: Relaxed everyday dialogue with an assistant, less formal than polite. Information: Retain all concrete values, amounts, units, target ranges, topk counts, requested activities, and action order. Allow limited meaning shifts in everyday wording, but never replace concrete amount with vague phrase. Terminology: Translate technical properties and operations into familiar expressions, allowing small everyday reinterpretations while keeping their concrete numeric details. : World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking References: Use the space/device layout to shorten names or omit unnecessary locations and device numbers when the intended target remains clear. Structure: Use natural questions, contractions, short leadins, and implicit references, expressing the overall request as person would in conversation. Avoid: Forced politeness, omitted numeric details, vague replacements for explicit goals, unrelated new objectives, and invented environment or userlocation facts. instruction_style_examples: Example 1: Input: Tell me the current temperature of the space named Kitchen. Rewrite: How hot is the kitchen right now? Example 2: Input: For Dining Room Lamp 8, decrease brightness by 10 and increase color_temperature by 300. (The dining room contains exactly one lamp, Dining Room Lamp 8. Other rooms may contain lamps.) Rewrite: Let's turn the dining room lamp's brightness down by 10 and make its color warmer by 300. Example 3: Input: Bring the illuminance in Stairs into line with Kate's saved preference. Rewrite: Let's bring the stairs' light level to Kate's usual setting. Example 4: Input: Compare current noise among Entryway, Laundry Room, Living Room; list every target in the top 2 positions for highest noise. Rewrite: Let's compare the noise in the entryway, laundry room, and living room right now. Tell me the top 2 noisiest rooms. Example 5: Input: Please change all bluetooth speaker devices as follows: adjust playback_content upward by 2 and adjust volume downward by 10. Then tell me the current temperature in Kitchen. Then, for all living_room spaces, work toward this outcome: increase their illuminance by about 100, ending between 780 and 820. Rewrite: Let's move playback content up by 2 and turn the volume down by 10 on all bluetooth speakers. Then tell me the temperature in the kitchen right now. After that, for all living rooms, let's raise the illuminance by about 100 so it ends between 780 and 820. F.2.5 Distracting Style REWRITE_STYLE_DISTRACTING instruction_style: distracting instruction_style_description: Tone: Relaxed everyday dialogue with an assistant, following conversational style while wandering into unrelated chatter. Information: Retain all concrete values, amounts, units, target ranges, topk counts, requested activities, dependencies, and action order. Allow the same limited everyday meaning shifts as conversational, but never replace concrete amount with vague phrase. Terminology: Translate technical properties and operations into familiar expressions while keeping their concrete numeric details. References: Use the space/device layout to shorten names or omit unnecessary locations and device numbers when the intended target remains clear. Structure: Add one or more asides before, between, or after task clauses. Vary the topic and placement naturally: today's experiences, feelings, tomorrow's plans, personal opinions or evaluations, or meaningless filler. Asides may describe the current environment, another environment, the device being controlled, or other devices. These details may be invented and may share the task's topic while remaining irrelevant to what the assistant should do. Avoid: Turning asides into additional requests, changes to task targets, conditions, deadlines, or scheduling instructions; inventing the user's current location; revealing query answers or private memory values; omitting task details. Keep task target references grounded in the supplied layout. Removing the asides must leave the same conversational request. instruction_style_examples: 61 : World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking Example 1: Input: Tell me the current temperature of the space named Kitchen. Rewrite: spent today tidying this kitchen and still can't decide whether like its layout. Anyway, how hot is the kitchen right now? Example 2: Input: For Dining Room Lamp 8, decrease brightness by 10 and increase color_temperature by 300. Layout: The dining room contains exactly one lamp, Dining Room Lamp 8. Other rooms may contain lamps. Rewrite: The dining room lamp's design reminds me of hotel stayed at; that trip always cheers me up. Let's turn the dining room lamp's brightness down by 10 and bump its color temperature up by 300. Example 3: Input: Bring the illuminance in Stairs into line with Kate's saved preference. Rewrite: Let's bring the stairs' light level to Kate's usual setting. I'm visiting our other office tomorrow; its stairwell always reminds me of my old school. Example 4: Input: Compare current noise among Entryway, Laundry Room, Living Room; list every target in the top 2 positions for highest noise. Rewrite: tried my friend's robot vacuum today. think its little voice prompts are hilarious. Let's compare the noise in the entryway, laundry room, and living room right now. Tell me the top 2 noisiest rooms. Example 5: Input: Please change all bluetooth speaker devices as follows: adjust playback_content upward by 2 and adjust volume downward by 10. Then tell me the current temperature in Kitchen. Then, for all living_room spaces, work toward this outcome: increase their illuminance by about 100, ending between 780 and 820. Rewrite: Let's move playback content up by 2 and turn the volume down by 10 on all bluetooth speakers. The air conditioner at yesterday's cafe looked like museum piece. Hmm, ladida, blah blah. Then tell me the temperature in the kitchen right now. After that, for all living rooms, let's raise the illuminance by about 100 so it ends between 780 and 820. F.2.6 Folk Style REWRITE_STYLE_FOLK instruction_style: folk instruction_style_description: Tone: Distinctly informal or regional speech, as in conversation with familiar neighbor; more colloquial than conversational. Information: Retain all concrete values, amounts, units, target ranges, topk counts, requested activities, and action order. Allow limited meaning shifts in everyday wording, but never replace concrete amount with vague phrase. Terminology: Use familiar slang and everyday descriptions of technical properties and operations, allowing small meaning shifts while keeping their concrete numeric details. References: Use the space/device layout to shorten names or omit unnecessary locations and device numbers when the intended target remains clear. Structure: Use contractions, dropped words, and regional turns of phrase consistently across the request, with natural local equivalents in its language. Avoid: Obscure dialect, heavy phonetic spelling, caricature, offensive language, omitted numeric details, vague replacements for explicit goals, unrelated new objectives, and invented environment facts. instruction_style_examples: Example 1: Input: Tell me the current temperature of the space named Kitchen. Rewrite: Hey, what's the temperature sittin' at in the kitchen right now? Example 2: Input: For Dining Room Lamp 8, decrease brightness by 10 and increase color_temperature by 300. Layout: The dining room contains exactly one lamp, Dining Room Lamp 8. Other rooms may contain lamps. Example 4: Input: Compare current noise among Entryway, Laundry Room, Living Room; list every target in the top 2 positions for highest noise. Example 5: Input: Please change all bluetooth speaker devices as follows: adjust playback_content upward by 2 and adjust volume downward by 10. Then tell me the current temperature in Kitchen. sections.title: Implicit Style
sections.content: REWRITE_STYLE_IMPLICIT instruction_style: implicit instruction_style_description: Tone: Indirect, intentfocused requests that leave details unstated, using natural everyday language. Information: Convey the broad user intent rather than every formal constraint. Approximation, omission, ambiguity, and some meaning shift are allowed, including qualitative goals instead of exact values or ranges. Terminology: Reinterpret technical properties and operations as user would describe the desired experience, without requiring literal or numerically equivalent translation. References: Ground the request in the space/device layout, allowing broader categories, omitted qualifiers, and contextual references even when the intended target is implicit rather than uniquely specified. Structure: Use natural questions, contractions, short leadins, and implicit references, expressing the overall request as person would in conversation. Avoid: Forced politeness, mechanical restatement of every parameter, unrelated new objectives, and invented environment or userlocation facts. instruction_style_examples: Example 1: Input: Tell me the current temperature of the space named Kitchen. Rewrite: How hot is the kitchen right now? Example 2: Input: For Dining Room Lamp 8, decrease brightness by 10 and increase color_temperature by 300. (The dining room contains exactly one lamp, Dining Room Lamp 8. Other rooms may contain lamps.) Rewrite: Let's make the dining room lamp little dimmer and warmer. Example 3: Input: Bring the illuminance in Stairs into line with Kate's saved preference. Rewrite: Let's get the stair lighting how Kate likes it. Example 4: Input: Compare current noise among Entryway, Laundry Room, Living Room; list every target in the top 2 positions for highest noise. Rewrite: Which of the entryway, laundry room, and living room are the noisiest two right now? Example 5: Input: Please change all bluetooth speaker devices as follows: adjust playback_content upward by 2 and adjust volume downward by 10. Then tell me the current temperature in Kitchen. Then, for all living_room spaces, work toward this outcome: increase their illuminance by about 100, ending between 780 and 820. Rewrite: Let's skip ahead couple of tracks and turn the bluetooth speakers down bit. Then tell me how hot it is in the kitchen. After that, brighten up all the living rooms. 63 : World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking F.3 ReAct Agent AGENT_SYSTEM_PROMPT You are devicecontrol assistant in SynthDCB. You need to explore the world and complete the user's task using the supplied tools, public task information, and observed tool call results. ## ReAct format You will work under the ReAct framework. The response of each turn must be wrapped in <answer> tags and contain exactly one Thought section and one Action section, following the structure below: <answer> Thought: <Analyze the task based on the interaction history and the latest observation, and determine which tools to call in this turn.> Action: [{"name": "<builtin tool name 1>", "arguments": {"<argument name 1>": "<argument value 1>", "<argument name 2>": "<argument value 2>", ...}}, ...] </answer> ## Task instructions Action must be one valid JSON array of calls to the listed builtin tools, preserving their argument schemas and JSON types. Request execution through this array only, without native toolcall syntax. Calls execute in array order after your response ends. Tool call results will be provided as observations in the next turn. Wait for those actual observations before choosing dependent actions. Never write, simulate, or assume an Observation, tool return value, later conversation turn, or successful execution. Never invent space/device IDs, function names, query answers, or state changes to continue the task. Invoke discovered device functions through `device_execute_action`. They are not additional builtin tools. Follow each tool's documented preconditions and argument formats. One task might contain several atom tasks. For tasks related to control, you can take actions one by one or simultaneously. For tasks related to queries, you should answer them in order through `session_submit_answer`, with one tool call per query. For infeasible tasks, you should submit report for each affected atom task through `session_submit_report`, with one tool call per atom task. Continue independent executable atom tasks. Use builtin tools with the prefix `memory_` for tasks related to memory. Use the observation's simulation time and `session_sleep_time` for timed actions. Device settings change through controls, while space properties may evolve gradually. Use `session_finish` when you want to end the interaction. response with an empty action list will also finish the interaction immediately. However, the simulator will continue evolving until the fixed duration has elapsed or the world's state becomes stable. Include exactly one Thought section and one Action section within the same and only <answer> block, with no Markdown fences, extra sections, or text after </answer>. Query tasks: Return raw typed property values, integer counts, or space_id/device_id string. Preserve raw listproperty order. Return target selections as arrays of exact device_id, space_id, and person IDs. Use [] for no matches. For ranking tasks, always include boundary ties. Therefore, the result may contain more targets than requested. Order ranking target IDs by the requested ranking first.
